chapters.title: Chapter 5: Agri Commodities and Base Metals

lessons.title: Base Metals: Copper, Aluminium and Zinc as Economic Signals

children.text: Traders have a nickname for copper: "Dr Copper", the metal with a PhD in economics. The idea is simple. Copper goes into wiring, power grids, buildings, cars and air conditioners, so when factories in China and elsewhere are busy, copper demand rises, and when they slow, it falls. Copper prices often turn before official growth data does. Aluminium and zinc tell similar stories with their own twists. By the end of this lesson you will understand what drives copper, aluminium and zinc, why China matters so much to all three, how MCX base metal prices are built from London Metal Exchange prices, and how these metals connect to Indian companies like Hindalco, Vedanta, Hindustan Zinc and cable makers.

body.text: Base metals are bets on the real economy. When construction, manufacturing and power investment expand, especially in China, they rise. When industrial activity slows, they fall. Precious metals respond to fear; base metals respond to growth.

children.text: Copper: The Economic Signal
Copper conducts electricity extremely well and is hard to substitute in most electrical uses. That places it at the centre of almost every kind of physical investment.
Construction and housing.
Wiring, plumbing and fittings. China's property sector has long been one of the largest single sources of demand.
Power grids and renewables.
Transmission lines, transformers, solar and wind installations all need large amounts of copper.
Electric vehicles.
An electric car uses several times more copper than a petrol or diesel car, in motors, batteries and wiring, plus the charging network around it.
Consumer durables.
Air conditioners, refrigerators and electronics.
Why Copper Leads the Economy
Businesses see orders rising.
Manufacturers and builders expect more activity.
They buy raw materials early.
Copper purchases for wiring, equipment and projects happen before output shows up in GDP data.
Copper prices respond quickly.
Futures markets react to purchasing managers' index (PMI) surveys, credit data and stimulus announcements the day they are released.
Official data follows.
Industrial production and GDP figures confirm the trend weeks or months later.

body.title: LME copper, annual average price (approximate, US dollars per tonne)

children.text: The jump in 2021 reflected the post-COVID recovery, huge stimulus spending and a rush of green energy investment. In May 2024, LME copper set a record above $11,000 a tonne, driven by expectations of demand from power grids and electric vehicles alongside supply disruptions, such as the closure of the large Cobre Panamá mine in late 2023.

body.text: Dr Copper's diagnosis is not always right. Copper can rally on supply problems, like mine closures or strikes, even when the economy is weak. It can also fall on Chinese policy headlines unrelated to global growth. Check whether a copper move is driven by demand or supply before reading it as an economic signal.

children.text: Aluminium: Metal Made From Electricity

Aluminium is produced by smelting alumina with enormous amounts of electricity, roughly 14 MWh for every tonne of metal. That makes aluminium prices unusually sensitive to energy costs. When European power prices spiked in 2022, several smelters there cut output because making aluminium had become unprofitable.

body.title: Power costs and aluminium
body.prompt: A smelter uses about 14 MWh of electricity to make one tonne of aluminium. If its power price rises from $40 per MWh to $90 per MWh, by how many US dollars does its electricity cost per tonne rise?
body.explanation: Increase in power price = $90 minus $40 = $50 per MWh. × 14 MWh = $700 per tonne. With LME aluminium at around $2,400 a tonne, that is close to 30% of the metal's price, enough to push high-cost smelters into losses.

children.text: China produces the majority of the world's aluminium, and India is the second-largest producer. Hindalco, Vedanta and NALCO have access to domestic bauxite and captive power, which is a key reason Indian producers are often among the lower-cost producers globally.
Zinc: Protecting Steel

markDefs.definition: Coating steel or iron with a layer of zinc to protect it from rust. It is the largest single use of zinc.

children.text: The largest use of zinc is
galvanising

, coating steel to stop it from rusting. That ties zinc demand closely to steel used in construction, infrastructure, vehicles and appliances. India's Hindustan Zinc, with mines in Rajasthan, is one of the world's large integrated zinc producers, and as you saw in Chapter 3, a major silver producer as a by-product.

body.title: Zinc's biggest job
body.textWithBlank: The largest use of zinc is ___, coating steel to protect it from rust.
body.explanation: Galvanised steel is used in construction, infrastructure, vehicles and appliances, which is why zinc demand tracks steel and building activity.

children.text: From LME to MCX: How Indian Prices Are Built
MCX base metal contracts are quoted in rupees per kg, while LME prices are in US dollars per tonne.

body.latex: \text{Price in INR per kg (before duty)} = \frac{\text{LME price in USD per tonne} \times \text{USD/INR}}{1{,}000}
body.caption: MCX prices also reflect import duty, freight and local premiums or discounts, so they typically sit somewhat above this converted figure.

body.title: Convert aluminium
body.prompt: LME aluminium is $2,400 per tonne and USD/INR is 85. What is the converted price in rupees per kg, before duty and premiums?
body.explanation: $2,400 × 85 = ₹2,04,000 per tonne. ÷ 1,000 kg = ₹204 per kg. Duty, freight and local premiums are added on top in the Indian market.

body.caption: MCX base metal futures (confirm current specifications on the MCX website)

body.text: Base metal contracts on MCX settle by physical delivery, as you learned in Chapter 2. They also react to Asian trading hours and Chinese data releases in the Indian morning and afternoon, not just to US data in the evening, which makes their rhythm different from crude oil and gold.

children.text: What Base Metal Traders Watch
China's PMIs.
Official and private manufacturing PMI surveys, released around the start of each month. A reading above 50 signals expansion; below 50 signals contraction.
China property and credit data.
New construction, home sales and lending growth.
Stimulus announcements.
Infrastructure spending or interest rate cuts in China can move metals sharply.
Exchange inventories.
Stocks in LME and Shanghai warehouses. Falling stocks suggest tightening supply.
Supply disruptions.
Mine strikes and closures for copper, and power shortages for aluminium smelters.
The US dollar.
As with other dollar-priced commodities, a weaker dollar tends to support prices.

body.title: When a metals market broke: LME nickel, March 2022

children.text: Nickel is another LME base metal, used in stainless steel and EV batteries. In early March 2022, after Russia's invasion of Ukraine raised fears over Russian nickel supply, prices surged. A large short position held by a Chinese nickel producer was caught in a squeeze.
Within a couple of trading sessions, nickel more than doubled and briefly traded above $100,000 a tonne.
On 8 March 2022, the LME suspended nickel trading and cancelled trades made earlier that day.
Trading stayed suspended for about a week, and the decision to cancel trades led to lawsuits and regulatory scrutiny.
The lesson echoes April 2020 in crude oil: in extreme conditions, liquidity can vanish, exchanges can intervene, and positions you believed were safe can behave in ways no model predicted.

body.label: India and copper
body.value: India turned from net exporter to net importer of refined copper
body.context: After Vedanta's Sterlite Copper smelter at Thoothukudi, Tamil Nadu, was shut in 2018 following protests, India's refined copper output fell and imports rose. New capacity, including Adani's Kutch Copper smelter, began coming onstream from 2024.

body.title: Read Dr Copper
body.question: Which combination of news is most likely to push copper prices down on demand concerns?
options: A major Chilean copper mine goes on strike
China's manufacturing PMI falls to 48 and new property construction keeps shrinking
China announces a large infrastructure stimulus package
body.explanation: A PMI below 50 signals manufacturing contraction, and shrinking construction cuts copper demand for wiring and fittings. A mine strike cuts supply, a weaker dollar supports prices, and stimulus raises demand expectations, so all three tend to push copper up.

body.title: Copper jumps on Chinese stimulus
body.scenario: Rhea, a 37-year-old investor in Chennai, holds shares of Hindalco and Polycab. One morning, China announces a large package of infrastructure and property support measures. LME copper rises 6% and aluminium 4%, and MCX copper follows. Her friend suggests she also buy 2 lots of MCX Copper futures "because China is back".
body.prompt: How might her two stocks react, and what should she consider before buying copper futures?
body.modelAnswer:
Stocks:
1. Hindalco is a producer of aluminium and copper products, so higher metal prices usually support its earnings and share price, although its large overseas aluminium rolling business responds to different factors too.
2. Polycab uses copper and aluminium as raw materials. A sudden jump can squeeze margins until it passes the increase on through price hikes, so the share may react negatively in the short term, even though stronger infrastructure spending could help demand over time.

Before buying copper futures:
1. Stimulus rallies can fade quickly if the details disappoint or implementation is slow. She would be buying after a 6% move.
2. Two Copper lots cover 5,000 kg. At around ₹850 per kg, that is about ₹42,50,000 of copper, and every ₹10 move is ₹50,000.
3. MCX copper settles by physical delivery, so she must roll or close before the delivery period.
4. She already has metals exposure through Hindalco, so futures would add to a similar bet rather than diversify.
5. If she wants to express the view, sizing should start from the loss she can accept on a realistic reversal.

points: Base metals track real economic activity, especially construction, manufacturing and power investment.
China consumes around half or more of global copper, aluminium and zinc, so Chinese data and policy move prices.
Copper often signals turns in growth, but supply shocks like mine closures can distort that signal.
Aluminium is an energy-intensive metal; zinc is tied to galvanised steel demand.
MCX prices are roughly LME USD per tonne × USD/INR ÷ 1,000, plus duty and premiums, and contracts settle by delivery.
Higher metal prices tend to help producers like Hindalco, Vedanta and Hindustan Zinc and squeeze consumers like cable makers.
